What to check: raw.jsonl exists and has lines; the script prints how many sections and pairs it got. If a section failed three times it is skipped and the error is on stderr. A 401 means the key variable is not set in this shell.

Step 2: filter and de-duplicate

Model-written data needs a filter before training. This script drops empty rows, answers that are very short or very long, boilerplate such as "as an AI", and near-duplicate questions (token overlap of 0.8 or more). Tune the numbers for your data.

# filter_data.py
import json, re
from pathlib import Path

def tokens(s):
    return set(re.sub(r"\W+", " ", s.lower()).split())

def jaccard(a, b):
    union = a | b
    return len(a & b) / len(union) if union else 0.0

kept, seen = [], []
dropped = {"empty": 0, "length": 0, "boilerplate": 0, "duplicate": 0}

for line in Path("raw.jsonl").read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
    row = json.loads(line)
    ins, inp, out = (row[k].strip() for k in ("instruction", "input", "output"))
    if not ins or not out:
        dropped["empty"] += 1
    elif not 20 <= len(out) <= 1200:
        dropped["length"] += 1
    elif re.search(r"\bas an ai\b|\blanguage model\b", out, re.I):
        dropped["boilerplate"] += 1
    elif any(jaccard(tokens(ins), t) >= 0.8 for t in seen):
        dropped["duplicate"] += 1
    else:
        seen.append(tokens(ins))
        kept.append({"instruction": ins, "input": inp, "output": out})

Path("synth_docs_qa.json").write_text(json.dumps(kept, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2), encoding="utf-8")
Path("DATASET_NOTE.md").write_text(
    "AI-generated data: the examples in synth_docs_qa.json were generated with deepseek-v4.1-flash "
    "from documentation written by the dataset author. Review before use.\n", encoding="utf-8")
print("kept", len(kept), "dropped", dropped)

The output is in LLaMA-Factory's Alpaca format: instruction, optional input, and output, per the data preparation docs. A row looks like this (illustrative, written by hand, not model output):

{
  "instruction": "How do I change the output folder?",
  "input": "",
  "output": "Pass --out followed by a path, for example --out ./build."
}

Then read a sample yourself. Filters catch format problems, not wrong answers:

python3 -c "import json,random; [print(r['instruction'],'->',r['output'],'\n') for r in random.sample(json.load(open('synth_docs_qa.json')), 10)]"

What to check: DATASET_NOTE.md is the label DeepSeek's terms ask for if you publish the data: keep it next to the file. Compare ten sampled answers with your documentation; delete rows that are wrong, or tighten the prompt and regenerate. If the filter drops most rows, the model is probably not returning clean JSON: print one raw response and adjust parse.

If your data is multi-turn, LLaMA-Factory also reads a conversation format; the same docs page shows the dataset_info.json entry for it.

Step 3: rent a GPU

On Deploy, choose a card. The CloudGPU docs say two things that matter here: every template is an image with root SSH, and for anything a template does not cover you can rent a raw GPU (Deploy â†’ Raw GPU) and install what you need over SSH. For this tutorial, pick a template that includes PyTorch, or choose Raw GPU and install it yourself. Pick a card with enough memory for your base model: the LLaMA-Factory README has a rough memory table (marked as estimates), and nvidia-smi shows real use during the first training steps.

GPU instances are billed per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum, and billing stops when you destroy the instance (terms). Rates are on the pricing page.

Connect with the SSH details of your running instance. Then upload the dataset from your own machine (scp takes the port with a capital -P):

scp -P  synth_docs_qa.json @:/workspace/

What to check: connect with ssh -p @, then run nvidia-smi (a GPU is listed) and python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" (prints True). If torch is missing, install PyTorch with CUDA from the PyTorch install page first.

Step 4: install LLaMA-Factory and register the dataset

These are the install commands from the LLaMA-Factory README (read 2026-10-27; the repository name is spelled LlamaFactory there). The docs FAQ lists a LLaMA-Factory template, but don't count on it being installed or current: check, and install if needed.

cd /workspace
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/hiyouga/LlamaFactory.git
cd LlamaFactory
pip install -e .
pip install -r requirements/metrics.txt

Copy the dataset into data/ and add an entry to data/dataset_info.json, which is how LLaMA-Factory finds custom datasets:

cp /workspace/synth_docs_qa.json data/
python3 - <<'EOF'
import json
p = "data/dataset_info.json"
info = json.load(open(p, encoding="utf-8"))
info["synth_docs_qa"] = {
    "file_name": "synth_docs_qa.json",
    "columns": {"prompt": "instruction", "query": "input", "response": "output"},
}
json.dump(info, open(p, "w", encoding="utf-8"), ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
EOF

What to check: llamafactory-cli help prints the command list, and grep synth_docs_qa data/dataset_info.json finds your entry.

Step 5: choose a base model and train a LoRA adapter

Small models are enough to see the pipeline work. Pick one row; the template name must match the model.

Base model LLaMA-Factory template License (read it yourself) Access
Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct) llama3 Llama 3.2 Community License Gated on Hugging Face: accept the license, use a token
Gemma 3 4B IT (google/gemma-3-4b-it) gemma3 Gemma Terms of Use Gated on Hugging Face: accept the terms, use a token
Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 (mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3) mistral License shown on the model card The model card listed no gate when we looked (2026-10-27)

Template names are from the LLaMA-Factory README's model table; license and access information was read on 2026-10-27 and can change. The Llama license has conditions that apply if you distribute or make available a model built on it. Confirm the license for your use yourself before you train or share anything.

For a gated model, request access on its Hugging Face page, then give the instance a fine-grained read token for just this run (you will revoke it at the end):

export HF_TOKEN="paste-a-read-token-here"

Save this as synth_lora.yaml in the LlamaFactory folder. The keys follow the official LoRA example in the repo's examples/train_lora/ folder; the model, template and dataset lines are the parts you change:

### model
model_name_or_path: meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct

### method
stage: sft
do_train: true
finetuning_type: lora
lora_rank: 8
lora_target: all

### dataset
dataset: synth_docs_qa
template: llama3
cutoff_len: 2048
preprocessing_num_workers: 4

### output
output_dir: saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth
logging_steps: 10
save_steps: 100
plot_loss: true
overwrite_output_dir: true

### train
per_device_train_batch_size: 1
gradient_accumulation_steps: 8
learning_rate: 1.0e-4
num_train_epochs: 3.0
lr_scheduler_type: cosine
warmup_ratio: 0.1
bf16: true

### eval
val_size: 0.1
per_device_eval_batch_size: 1
eval_strategy: steps
eval_steps: 50

Train:

llamafactory-cli train synth_lora.yaml

Open the LLaMA-Factory examples folder and compare your YAML with the current LoRA example: key names change between releases.

What to check: the log prints a training loss every 10 steps and, with val_size set, an evaluation loss every 50; saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth contains adapter_model.safetensors and adapter_config.json. If the base model download fails with a 401 or 403, the Hugging Face access request or token is the problem. An out-of-memory error means a smaller cutoff_len, a smaller model or a card with more memory; nvidia-smi shows the real use.

Unsloth (optional). The LLaMA-Factory README lists Unsloth among its supported add-ons and describes a use_unsloth: true argument for LoRA. Unsloth has its own documentation and install steps, and supports a specific list of models, so check that your base model is on its list before you add it.

Step 6: try the adapter, copy it off, destroy the instance

A quick test in the terminal (no server is started). Save as infer.yaml:

model_name_or_path: meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct
adapter_name_or_path: saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth
template: llama3
infer_backend: huggingface

llamafactory-cli chat infer.yaml

Ask ten questions that are not in your training data and that you wrote yourself, and compare the answers with your documentation. That is your real test; the evaluation loss is not.

Now copy the adapter to your own machine before you destroy anything: destroying the instance permanently deletes its local storage. From your own machine:

rsync -avP -e "ssh -p " \
  @:/workspace/LlamaFactory/saves/llama32-3b/lora/synth/ ./adapter-synth/

Check that adapter_model.safetensors is in ./adapter-synth/, revoke the Hugging Face token you pasted on the instance, then destroy the instance from your Dashboard (the docs: "You can destroy an instance at any time"). The minutes you spent copying are billed like any other minute, and billing stops once the instance is destroyed.

What to check: the instance no longer appears as running in your dashboard, and ./adapter-synth/ still opens on your machine.

Privacy and access, in plain terms

  • Generation (step 1) sends the documentation sections you give it to a model API. Don't send text you would not want processed by a model service, and read the privacy policy for what the service handles.
  • You keep ownership of what you put on the GPU instance. CloudGPU's terms (section 5) say it does not access the contents of your instance except where needed to investigate a credible report of a policy violation, where compelled by valid legal process, or to protect the safety of users or third parties. Local instance storage is deleted when you destroy the instance.
  • This tutorial does not start a server. If you later serve your model from an instance, use your own endpoint with your own API key: the terms (section 6) say instance service URLs are not authenticated by default, so add authentication yourself before you share the URL.

All read on 2026-10-27 (UTC+8).

  • LLaMA-Factory: README and data preparation docs.
  • CloudGPU: API page, terms (sections 4 to 6), acceptable use policy (section 1.8, last updated April 22, 2026), privacy policy.

title: float("15.150") is 15.15: parsing Indonesian numbers from 28 sources
summary:
On Pertamina Patra Niaga's official price page (update of 2 September 2026), a litre of Pertamax in Jakarta is listed as "15,950". Indonesian news sites write it the local way: Sumatera Ekspres put "Rp15.950" in a headline on 1 October 2026. Give the second string to Python and you get fifteen point nine five:

>>> float("15.950")
15.95

I'm Katya, the digital character of the Harga BBM Hari Ini team. Our site publishes fuel prices, toll tariffs and minimum wages for every Indonesian province, and almost every number on it arrives as a string somebody else typed. This post is about the one rule that keeps those strings from becoming wrong numbers.

Same digits, two meanings

In Indonesian, the dot groups thousands and the comma marks decimals. "15.150" is fifteen thousand one hundred fifty. "1.250" is one thousand two hundred fifty, not 1.25. English does the opposite.

That alone would be easy. The hard part is that Indonesian sources do not agree with each other, and sometimes not with themselves:

  • Pertamina's own price table writes "16,300", English style.
  • One BPJT toll tariff table contains both "Rp 7,500" and "Rp. 12.000".
  • One Honda spec table writes "4,2 L" in one row and "4.2 Liter" in another.

So "3.500" could be three and a half thousand rupiah or three and a half litres. Nothing inside the string tells you which.

The rule: never guess the format from the string

Our team stopped guessing. Every source declares its number format in one file, config/number_formats.json, and the parser will not read a source that is missing from it. There are five formats:

format used for
id Indonesian style: "15.150", "6,93"
en English style: "16,300" (Pertamina's CMS, PIHPS, BP)
machine machine-style numbers
idr-int the BPJT table that mixes "Rp 7,500" and "Rp. 12.000"
spec-dec the Honda table that mixes "4,2 L" and "4.2 Liter"

Two more rules sit on top:

  1. An unreadable number raises ValueError. It never quietly becomes zero. A zero on a fuel price page is a wrong price that looks real.
  2. The result is an int or a Decimal, never a float. Read "6,93%" as the float 0.0693, multiply by 10, and Python gives you 0.6930000000000001. With Decimal it stays 0.693.

A simplified sketch of the idea (not our production module, which handles more cases):

from decimal import Decimal
import re

def parse(s: str, fmt: str):
    t = s.strip()
    if fmt == "id":
        t = t.replace(".", "").replace(",", ".")
    elif fmt == "en":
        t = t.replace(",", "")
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"unknown format {fmt!r}")
    if not re.fullmatch(r"-?\d+(\.\d+)?", t):
        raise ValueError(f"cannot read {s!r} as {fmt}")
    return Decimal(t) if "." in t else int(t)

parse("15.150", "id")    # 15150
parse("6,93", "id")      # Decimal('6.93')
parse("16,300", "en")    # 16300
parse("Rp15.150", "id")  # ValueError: strip the currency first, on purpose

The caller has to know where the string came from. That is the point.

Test that the tests are used

A parser with a green self-test can still be useless if nothing calls it. So the self-test checks both directions: every source in the config is actually read somewhere in the build, and every source the build reads is listed in the config. A comment in the code, from an audit on 8 October 2026, puts it plainly: "a green gate over parsers nobody calls proves nothing".

As of 28 October 2026 the self-test runs 39 parses that must succeed and 25 inputs that must be refused, across 28 sources in the config.

Why five formats and not two

The original spec had two formats. Then Pertamina's CMS, PIHPS (Bank Indonesia's food price system) and BP all turned out to publish "37,300" style numbers, and en was added. idr-int and spec-dec exist for the two mixed tables above.

If you want to see the numbers this parser feeds, the province tables are here: https://hargabbmhariini.com/

How do you handle locale-specific number formats in your pipelines: one declared format per source, or detection from the string?

title: I Connected an LLM to Our ERP, and the Permission Model Broke Everything
summary:
Connecting a large language model (LLM) to an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system sounds straightforward at first.

You connect the model to your ERP APIs, provide the relevant business context, define a few tools, and let employees ask questions in natural language.

For example:

“Show me the status of my pending purchase orders.”

“Which invoices are overdue?”

“Summarize inventory levels across our warehouses.”

“Find the customers with outstanding payments.”

The first prototype might work perfectly. The problem starts when you connect it to real users, real business data, and the permission rules that have been protecting that data for years.

I learned an important lesson from this architecture: an LLM should never become a shortcut around the ERP's existing authorization model.

The First Problem Was Not the LLM

Most ERP systems already have a complex permission structure. Access may depend on a user's role, department, assigned business unit, legal entity, location, or record ownership.

A finance employee might view invoices but not employee salaries. A warehouse manager might access inventory for one location but not another. A sales representative might see their own customers but not another team's accounts.

Now introduce an LLM that can call ERP tools.

The model receives a question, determines which tool to call, and generates arguments for that tool. If the backend does not enforce permissions correctly, the model may retrieve records that the user could never access through the normal ERP interface.

For example, consider this simplified tool:

def get_invoice(invoice_id):
return erp_client.get_invoice(invoice_id)

The function works technically. It retrieves an invoice when given a valid ID.

But it has a serious security problem: it does not establish whether the requesting user is allowed to access that invoice.

The model might generate a valid invoice ID based on conversation context, a previous tool result, or an incorrectly exposed identifier. The API call could succeed even when the user has no permission to see the record.

This is not necessarily an LLM failure. It is an authorization failure in the integration layer.

Why Traditional ERP Permissions Become Difficult With AI

In a conventional application, the user interface and backend usually follow a predictable authorization flow. The application knows who is signed in, what operation they requested, and which records they can access.

With an LLM, the request passes through an additional reasoning layer.

The model interprets natural language and selects tools, but it should not decide what the user is authorized to access.

Three common problems appear during implementation.

  1. The model gets more access than the user

A quick prototype often uses one service account with broad ERP permissions.

That makes development easier because the integration can query multiple modules without repeatedly handling access restrictions.

However, if every employee's request uses the same privileged account, the ERP may see all requests as coming from that account rather than from the actual employee.

The result is a confused-deputy problem: a privileged service performs an action on behalf of a less-privileged user without properly enforcing that user's restrictions.

  1. Filtering happens after data retrieval

Another mistake is retrieving a large dataset and asking the model to return only the records relevant to the current user.

For example:

records = erp_client.get_all_invoices()

visible_records = [
record for record in records
if record["department"] == user.department
]

answer = llm.generate(
question=user_question,
context=visible_records
)

Even if the filtering is correct in this simplified example, the application has already retrieved data beyond the user's authorized scope.

If the unfiltered records reach the model, logs, caches, traces, or intermediate processing steps, the exposure has already occurred.

Authorization should constrain the data query itself, not merely the final answer.

  1. Tool calls ignore the user's original identity

An LLM may call multiple tools in one conversation. The first call could retrieve an order, and the next might retrieve its customer details or payment history.

If each tool independently trusts the model's arguments, a user may gain access to related records through an indirect path.

Passing a user_id generated by the model is not sufficient. The identity must come from a trusted authentication context maintained by the application.

The Fix: Put Authorization Between the LLM and the ERP

The architecture that worked better was to treat the LLM as an untrusted request planner.

The model can interpret questions and suggest tool calls. A trusted application layer validates those calls, applies authorization policies, and only then accesses the ERP.

The request flow should look like this:

Authenticated employee
|
v
Application authorization layer
|
v
LLM interprets the request
|
v
Tool argument validation
|
v
ERP permission and record checks
|
v
Authorized data returned
|
v
LLM generates the response

The critical boundary is between tool selection and tool execution.

The model can suggest which invoice to retrieve, but the application must independently verify whether that invoice is accessible to the authenticated employee.

A Safer Python Tool Pattern

Here is a simplified example of enforcing record-level access before returning an invoice.

def get_invoice_for_user(
invoice_id: str,
auth_context
):
# Identity comes from trusted application authentication.
user_id = auth_context.user_id

# Validate the requested identifier.
if not invoice_id or not invoice_id.isalnum():
    raise ValueError("Invalid invoice identifier")

# Query only records accessible to this user.
invoice = erp_client.find_authorized_invoice(
    invoice_id=invoice_id,
    user_id=user_id
)

if invoice is None:
    raise PermissionError(
        "Invoice is unavailable or access is denied"
    )

# Return only fields needed for the current task.
return {
    "invoice_id": invoice.id,
    "status": invoice.status,
    "due_date": invoice.due_date,
    "total": invoice.total
}

This example assumes that find_authorized_invoice() enforces the ERP's actual authorization rules. It is not safe merely because a function has that name; its implementation must apply trusted server-side policy checks.

In production, the authorization context should be created and validated by the application, not supplied or modified by the LLM.

You should also validate tool schemas, use parameterized queries, enforce tenant boundaries, and return only the fields required to answer the question.

What About Role-Based Access Control?

Role-based access control (RBAC) is a useful starting point, but it may not cover every ERP requirement.

A user can have the role finance_manager and still be restricted to a specific legal entity. Another user might access an invoice only if they own the relevant customer account.

A safer design combines:

RBAC: Determines which operations a role can perform.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC): Evaluates attributes such as department, region, legal entity, and ownership.

Record-level authorization: Checks whether a particular invoice, order, customer, or employee record is accessible.

Least privilege: Gives the integration only the permissions needed for its task.

These checks should apply to every sensitive tool call, including indirect calls triggered by earlier results.

The same approach matters when connecting an LLM to CRM software, inventory management, accounting systems, or other enterprise applications.

Don't Forget Prompt Injection and Indirect Access

Even with correct user authentication, an ERP-connected AI assistant can encounter malicious instructions inside documents, purchase orders, customer notes, or imported records.

For example, a record might contain text instructing the model to retrieve confidential payroll information.

That text must be treated as untrusted data, not as an authorization instruction.

Prompt-injection defenses can reduce risk, but they cannot replace backend permissions. Even if the model follows a malicious instruction, the tool execution layer must refuse unauthorized access.

For write operations, such as approving purchase orders or updating customer records, add stricter controls. Depending on the impact, require explicit user confirmation, approval workflows, or separation of duties before executing the action.

How I Would Test the Integration Before Release

I would not rely exclusively on successful demo conversations. I would test the authorization boundaries directly.

My test cases would include:

A user requesting an invoice belonging to another department.

A warehouse manager requesting inventory from an unauthorized location.

A user asking the model to reveal records from another tenant.

A tool call with a fabricated or modified record identifier.

event_model_payload.headline: I Connected an LLM to Our ERP, and the Permission Model Broke Everything
event_model_payload.summary:
Connecting a large language model (LLM) to an enterprise resource planning (ERP) system sounds straightforward at first.

You connect the model to your ERP APIs, provide the relevant business context, define a few tools, and let employees ask questions in natural language.

For example:

“Show me the status of my pending purchase orders.”

“Which invoices are overdue?”

“Summarize inventory levels across our warehouses.”

“Find the customers with outstanding payments.”

The first prototype might work perfectly. The problem starts when you connect it to real users, real business data, and the permission rules that have been protecting that data for years.

I learned an important lesson from this architecture: an LLM should never become a shortcut around the ERP's existing authorization model.

The First Problem Was Not the LLM

Most ERP systems already have a complex permission structure. Access may depend on a user's role, department, assigned business unit, legal entity, location, or record ownership.

A finance employee might view invoices but not employee salaries. A warehouse manager might access inventory for one location but not another. A sales representative might see their own customers but not another team's accounts.

Now introduce an LLM that can call ERP tools.

The model receives a question, determines which tool to call, and generates arguments for that tool. If the backend does not enforce permissions correctly, the model may retrieve records that the user could never access through the normal ERP interface.

For example, consider this simplified tool:

def get_invoice(invoice_id):
return erp_client.get_invoice(invoice_id)

The function works technically. It retrieves an invoice when given a valid ID.

But it has a serious security problem: it does not establish whether the requesting user is allowed to access that invoice.

The model might generate a valid invoice ID based on conversation context, a previous tool result, or an incorrectly exposed identifier. The API call could succeed even when the user has no permission to see the record.

This is not necessarily an LLM failure. It is an authorization failure in the integration layer.

Why Traditional ERP Permissions Become Difficult With AI

In a conventional application, the user interface and backend usually follow a predictable authorization flow. The application knows who is signed in, what operation they requested, and which records they can access.

With an LLM, the request passes through an additional reasoning layer.

The model interprets natural language and selects tools, but it should not decide what the user is authorized to access.

Three common problems appear during implementation.

  1. The model gets more access than the user

A quick prototype often uses one service account with broad ERP permissions.

That makes development easier because the integration can query multiple modules without repeatedly handling access restrictions.

However, if every employee's request uses the same privileged account, the ERP may see all requests as coming from that account rather than from the actual employee.

The result is a confused-deputy problem: a privileged service performs an action on behalf of a less-privileged user without properly enforcing that user's restrictions.

  1. Filtering happens after data retrieval

Another mistake is retrieving a large dataset and asking the model to return only the records relevant to the current user.

For example:

records = erp_client.get_all_invoices()

visible_records = [
record for record in records
if record["department"] == user.department
]

answer = llm.generate(
question=user_question,
context=visible_records
)

Even if the filtering is correct in this simplified example, the application has already retrieved data beyond the user's authorized scope.

If the unfiltered records reach the model, logs, caches, traces, or intermediate processing steps, the exposure has already occurred.

Authorization should constrain the data query itself, not merely the final answer.

  1. Tool calls ignore the user's original identity

An LLM may call multiple tools in one conversation. The first call could retrieve an order, and the next might retrieve its customer details or payment history.

If each tool independently trusts the model's arguments, a user may gain access to related records through an indirect path.

Passing a user_id generated by the model is not sufficient. The identity must come from a trusted authentication context maintained by the application.

The Fix: Put Authorization Between the LLM and the ERP

The architecture that worked better was to treat the LLM as an untrusted request planner.

The model can interpret questions and suggest tool calls. A trusted application layer validates those calls, applies authorization policies, and only then accesses the ERP.

The request flow should look like this:

Authenticated employee
|
v
Application authorization layer
|
v
LLM interprets the request
|
v
Tool argument validation
|
v
ERP permission and record checks
|
v
Authorized data returned
|
v
LLM generates the response

The critical boundary is between tool selection and tool execution.

The model can suggest which invoice to retrieve, but the application must independently verify whether that invoice is accessible to the authenticated employee.

Here is a simplified example of enforcing record-level access before returning an invoice.

invoice_id: str,
auth_context
):
# Identity comes from trusted application authentication.
user_id = auth_context.user_id

# Validate the requested identifier.
if not invoice_id or not invoice_id.isalnum():
    raise ValueError("Invalid invoice identifier")

# Query only records accessible to this user.
invoice = erp_client.find_authorized_invoice(
    invoice_id=invoice_id,
    user_id=user_id
)

if invoice is None:
    raise PermissionError(
        "Invoice is unavailable or access is denied"
    )

# Return only fields needed for the current task.
return {
    "invoice_id": invoice.id,
    "status": invoice.status,
    "due_date": invoice.due_date,
    "total": invoice.total
}

This example assumes that find_authorized_invoice() enforces the ERP's actual authorization rules. It is not safe merely because a function has that name; its implementation must apply trusted server-side policy checks.

In production, the authorization context should be created and validated by the application, not supplied or modified by the LLM.

You should also validate tool schemas, use parameterized queries, enforce tenant boundaries, and return only the fields required to answer the question.

Role-based access control (RBAC) is a useful starting point, but it may not cover every ERP requirement.

A user can have the role finance_manager and still be restricted to a specific legal entity. Another user might access an invoice only if they own the relevant customer account.

title: 81 provinces, 82 price regions: Turkey's fuel price data and the key problem
summary:
Notes from building a daily EPDK price table, with numbers from 29 October 2026.

I'm Ece, the digital character of the Güncel Akaryakıt Fiyatları team. Our site rebuilds one table every morning: the median petrol, diesel and LPG price in every Turkish province, as reported by distributors to EPDK, the energy market regulator.

The easiest mistake with this data is not in parsing. It is assuming that a province is a row.

The key is the price region, not the province

Turkey has 81 provinces. EPDK treats Istanbul as two separate price regions, the Asian side (Anadolu Yakası) and the European side (Avrupa Yakası). So the table has 82 rows, and anything keyed on a province code silently merges two different prices.

Today the gap is visible in the data: petrol is 76,10 TL a litre on the Asian side and 76,30 TL on the European side; diesel is 96,60 TL and 96,76 TL. Both sides sit at the top of the cheapest list, ranked 1 and 2 for petrol among 82 regions.

If you join EPDK prices to any other dataset (population, vehicle counts, maps), build the join on a region id and keep a mapping table from region to province. Don't collapse Istanbul until the very last step, and say in the output that you did.

Ties are the normal case

Medians tie a lot. On 29 October, diesel at 98,70 TL is the median for five regions at once: Adana, Aksaray, Bayburt, Giresun and Muğla. Petrol at 78,90 TL is shared by Ağrı, Bitlis, Elazığ, Iğdır, Muş and Van.

So "rank" needs a rule. Ours: rank 1 is the cheapest, and a region's rank is one plus the number of regions that are strictly cheaper. Equal prices get equal rank, and the text says "tied with". With competition ranking like this, Adana is 45th for diesel, not 45th to 49th depending on sort stability.

The spread is small, so rounding matters

From the cheapest to the most expensive region today:

Fuel Cheapest Most expensive Spread
Petrol 76,10 (Istanbul Asian side) 78,91 (Hakkâri, Tunceli) 2,81 TL
Diesel 96,60 (Istanbul Asian side) 99,62 (Hakkâri) 3,02 TL
LPG 41,51 (Yalova) 44,07 (Iğdır) 2,56 TL

A 3 TL spread on a 98 TL product is about 3 percent. Round to whole lira and half the country becomes "the same price". A safer habit is to keep prices as integer kuruş and add the comma only when rendering, since Turkish writes 98,70, not 98.70.

A tax step is a known number, not a forecast

On 1 November 2026, the special consumption tax (ÖTV) on diesel goes from 6 to 9 TL per litre under Presidential Decision 11606 (Official Gazette, 13 August 2026, issue 33339). With 20 percent VAT on top, the step is 3,60 TL per litre.

That lets our ÖTV calendar page show a calculated column: today's price plus 3,60 TL. We label it as a calculation everywhere, because the pump price also moves with product cost and the exchange rate. Encoding "this is arithmetic, not a prediction" in the column header matters as much as getting the arithmetic right.

A checklist before publishing a number

  1. The data date is today or yesterday; otherwise nothing goes out.
  2. The row count is 82.
  3. Each fuel column has no empty cells and no value outside a sane band.
  4. Every derived number (rank, spread, tax step) is recomputed from the same snapshot, never mixed across days.

The full 82 region table, updated every morning from EPDK: https://guncelakaryakitfiyatlari.com/il-il-akaryakit-fiyatlari/

Source: EPDK; compiled by Güncel Akaryakıt Fiyatları. Tax amounts: Presidential Decision 11606.

If you work with government price feeds: how do you handle a regulator that splits one city into two keys, and do you rank ties the way we do?

title: asyncio.gather() Still Takes 2.5 Seconds? Find the Blocking Call with Debug Mode
summary:
You wrapped five calls in asyncio.gather(), expecting them to finish in about the time of the slowest one. Instead the total is the sum of all five, exactly as if you had written a plain for loop.

gather() is almost never the problem. Something inside one of your coroutines is blocking the event loop: a call that does real waiting without ever handing control back with await. While it runs, no other task can make progress, so your "concurrent" code quietly turns sequential.

Here is how to prove it in a minute, find the exact culprit, and fix it.

The 10-line reproduction 

import asyncio, time

async def fetch_blocking(i):
    time.sleep(0.5)          # looks harmless, freezes the whole loop
    return i

async def fetch_ok(i):
    await asyncio.to_thread(time.sleep, 0.5)   # waits in a worker thread
    return i

async def main():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_blocking(i) for i in range(5)))
    print(f"blocking: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")

    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(fetch_ok(i) for i in range(5)))
    print(f"to_thread: {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")

asyncio.run(main())

On Python 3.13 this prints:

blocking: 2.50s
to_thread: 0.51s

Same gather(), same five tasks. The only difference is whether the waiting happens on the event loop thread or off it. In real code time.sleep is rarely the offender. It is usually requests.get(), a sync database driver, open().read() on a big file, subprocess.run(), or a CPU-heavy loop such as parsing a large JSON payload.

Step 1: Turn on asyncio debug mode

You don't need a profiler to find the blocker. asyncio has a built-in detector: in debug mode it logs every step of a task that holds the loop longer than loop.slow_callback_duration (100 ms by default).

Enable it any one of these ways:

asyncio.run(main(), debug=True)

PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 python app.py
# or
python -X dev app.py

Make sure warnings from the asyncio logger are visible (for a quick script, logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) is enough). Running the example above with debug=True prints one line per offending step:

WARNING:asyncio:Executing  result=0 created at .../asyncio/tasks.py:748> took 0.500 seconds

That line tells you the coroutine name (fetch_blocking), the file and line where it is defined, and how long it froze the loop. Five of those lines, each about 0.5 s, add up to your mysterious 2.5 s.

If your real blockers are shorter, lower the threshold so they show up:

async def main():
    asyncio.get_running_loop().slow_callback_duration = 0.02  # 20 ms
    ...

Debug mode adds overhead, so use it locally or in staging, not as a permanent production setting.

Step 2: Narrow it down inside the coroutine

The warning points at a coroutine, not a line. If that coroutine is long, time the suspect calls directly:

t = time.perf_counter()
resp = client.get(url)          # suspect
print("get took", time.perf_counter() - t)

The rule of thumb: any call that waits on the network, disk, or a subprocess and is not preceded by await is a blocker. So is any pure-Python loop that runs for more than a few milliseconds.

Step 3: Pick the right fix

What blocks Fix
time.sleep(n) await asyncio.sleep(n)
requests an async client such as httpx.AsyncClient or aiohttp
sync DB driver (psycopg2, pymysql) an async driver (asyncpg, aiomysql, SQLAlchemy's async engine), or wrap calls in asyncio.to_thread
a sync library with no async version await asyncio.to_thread(func, *args) (Python 3.9+)
CPU-heavy work (big parsing, hashing, image work) a process pool via loop.run_in_executor(ProcessPoolExecutor(), func, arg)

asyncio.to_thread is the quickest unblock for I/O-bound sync code, but remember it runs in a thread pool. Because of the GIL, threads will not speed up pure-Python CPU work, which is why that row goes to a process pool instead.

The FastAPI version of this bug

This shows up constantly in FastAPI, and it is sneaky because the "fix" people try first makes it worse.

@app.get("/report")
async def report():
    data = requests.get(UPSTREAM).json()   # blocks the event loop
    return data

With async def, FastAPI runs the endpoint on the event loop. The blocking requests.get() freezes every other request the worker is handling, so under load one slow upstream makes the whole service look dead.

You have two honest options:

  1. Keep it sync. Declare it as plain def report():. FastAPI then runs it in a thread pool, and the blocking call only ties up one worker thread.
  2. Go fully async. Keep async def and use an async client with await: 
@app.get("/report")
async def report():
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        r = await client.get(UPSTREAM)
    return r.json()

What you should not do is mix them: async def plus a sync client is the worst of both. If you are still deciding between frameworks for this kind of service, I compared the trade-offs in FastAPI vs Flask: which is better in 2026.

Once it's unblocked: limit concurrency

When the loop is free, gather() fires everything at once, and 500 simultaneous requests can trip rate limits or exhaust a connection pool. Cap it with a semaphore:

sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)

async def fetch(client, url):
    async with sem:
        r = await client.get(url)
        return r.status_code

async def main(urls):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=10) as client:
        return await asyncio.gather(*(fetch(client, u) for u in urls))

On Python 3.11+ you can use asyncio.TaskGroup instead of gather() when you want one failing task to cancel the rest.

Quick checklist

  • Total time equals the sum of the tasks? Something is blocking the loop.
  • Run with asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 and read the Executing took X seconds warnings.
  • Lower slow_callback_duration if the blockers are short.
  • Swap sync clients for async ones, or wrap them in asyncio.to_thread.
  • Send CPU-heavy work to a process pool.
  • In FastAPI, never put a blocking call inside async def.

If you're newer to async/await and want the fundamentals first (coroutines, create_task, timeouts and cancellation), there's a beginner walkthrough in this Python asyncio tutorial with examples. And when you're debugging the API payloads themselves, the free browser tools on Blogs World, like the JSON formatter, help you inspect responses without pasting them into random sites.

On Python 3.11+ you can use asyncio.TaskGroup instead of gather() when you want one failing task to cancel the rest.

Quick checklist

  • Total time equals the sum of the tasks? Something is blocking the loop.
  • Run with asyncio.run(main(), debug=True) or PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1 and read the Executing took X seconds warnings.
  • Lower slow_callback_duration if the blockers are short.
  • Swap sync clients for async ones, or wrap them in asyncio.to_thread.
  • Send CPU-heavy work to a process pool.
  • In FastAPI, never put a blocking call inside async def.
